nodes.title: Auditable Human-Agent Teams for Autonomous X-ray Experimentation
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.12933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Closed-loop autonomous experimentation can accelerate scientific discovery, but implementation effort limits accessibility. Agentic ...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.12933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Closed-loop autonomous experimentation can accelerate scientific discovery, but implementation effort limits accessibility. Agentic systems may lower this barrier, although sustained operation on physical instruments remains largely unexplored. Here, using coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, we demonstrate autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments on nanoparticle superlattices under evolving, human-defined objectives. Complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts enable an audit that reconstructs decision provenance and characterizes the division of cognitive labor. Across three experiments, 61-67% of messages involved interpretation or judgment, while the share of methodological and scientific contributions increased from 46% in the setup-focused first experiment to 56-61% in later experiments. Provenance showed that 59-68% of error corrections involved multiple participants and that about half of all decisions incorporated the input of another participant. These results may guide design principles for multi-agent scientific systems and inform future agent harnesses, model training, and accessible autonomous experimentation.

nodes.title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imager
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.12934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reli...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.12934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

nodes.title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.12935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topic monitoring is the task of labelling the topic of each token in a model's response during generation. Activation-based monitors...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.12935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topic monitoring is the task of labelling the topic of each token in a model's response during generation. Activation-based monitors that run at generation time have so far been trained to detect harmful content and are limited to two or three classes. We introduce TopicScope, a framework for training causal topic classifiers on SAE features that assign a topic to every token, so that the label can change partway through a response. We train three detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics. Across Gemma-3 1B and 4B, monitors trained on features extracted from prefill hidden states were able to generalise to decoding. We also found that the classifiers are robust to perturbations, losing at most 5 macro-F1 points when off-topic asides are inserted, topics are removed or sections are reordered. Ablations conducted to understand the contribution of the SAE revealed that classifiers reaching baseline performance without it were several times larger. Our findings show that compact topic monitors can be trained inexpensively in prefill and deployed during generation. More broadly, our work shows where SAEs are useful beyond safety classification. Our code, dataset and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mercity-AI/SAE-Guardrails and https://huggingface.co/collections/Mercity/online-guardrails-using-sparse-autoencoders-6ac602940468c62fefb2b9e8

nodes.title: LandslideFM: A Foundation Model Towards Unified Landslide Perception and Understanding
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.12936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual ta...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.12936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.

nodes.title: Tracing Psychometric Inference in Large Language Models
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.12937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do large language models represent psychological constructs internally, or do they only generate outputs that resemble psychometric ...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.12937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do large language models represent psychological constructs internally, or do they only generate outputs that resemble psychometric structure? We address this question using a cross-persona paradigm across 14 model variants from two families (Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5, 0.5B-14B, base and instruct). Given responses on one psychological scale from real individuals (N = 272 Taiwanese university students), models predict responses on six other scales. At the behavioral level, larger variants reproduce and amplify human cross-scale correlations; amplification persists after correcting the seven-scale human correlations for measurement attenuation. We then examine whether this structure is reflected internally. Contrastive direction analysis finds geometry aligned with the human matrix in larger instruct variants, but little alignment in base variants under this assay. Across models, geometry strength is associated with behavioral amplification (r = 0.68, p = 0.008; partial r = 0.69 controlling for log size). To relate internal structure to output behavior, a matched activation-probing paradigm shows that probe slopes vary less than behavioral slopes (1.38-1.77 vs 0.52-1.53). A synthetic control shows that ridge probing can inflate these slopes; after subtracting a baseline based on a reliability proxy from another analysis, adjusted slopes remain associated with behavior (r = 0.88). We term the measured probe-behavior gap readout attenuation. These results establish decodability and geometric alignment under the tested assays, without showing that the measured directions mediate the cross-persona answers.

nodes.title: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
nodes.tldr: CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Rest...
nodes.details: CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability  CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability  CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability  CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability  CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability  CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

nodes.title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
nodes.tldr: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-re...
nodes.details: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available.  Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts.  Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC.  Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

nodes.title: US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems
nodes.tldr: Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA),...
nodes.details: Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization. The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access. Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards. Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors: Authentication bypass; Arbitrary code injection; and Weak configurations. Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects: Change of temperature, which could: Affect the service life of the system; Create a fire hazard; Cause loss of inventory; or Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage. Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition). Mitigations The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement: Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices. Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I]. Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F]. Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance. Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H]. Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O]. Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity. For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets. Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations. Resources The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations: CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT Contact Information The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet: Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident: Date, time, and location of the incident; Type of activity; Number of people affected; Type of equipment used for the activity; and Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact. Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts. nodes.title: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful
nodes.tldr: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/06/2026 - 12:09 The Euro...
nodes.details: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/06/2026 - 12:09 The European Commission has preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the so-called ‘rabbit hole effect’ of its recommender system. TikTok's ‘For You' feed shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image. The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's ‘For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image. These ‘rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors. These preliminary findings focus on both risk assessment and mitigation measures. nodes.title: Independent study on the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and costs for businesses
nodes.tldr: Independent study on the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and costs for businesses Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 15:04 An independent study analyses the i...
nodes.details: Independent study on the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and costs for businesses Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 15:04 An independent study analyses the impacts of age assurance on fundamental rights and the costs for businesses concerned. Age assurance is key for a safer online environment as it ensures that children only access online services and features that are safe and age appropriate for them. Nowadays, 1 in 3 children, aged 9 to 11 across 6 European countries, reports having a social media profile. Very few services are implementing age assurance in a systematic way. To further strengthen the preparation of the proposed EU KIDS Act and the accompanying Staff Working Document, the European Commission procured a study to: Analyse the impact of age assurance on key fundamental rights, including data protection and privacy, non-discrimination, freedom of expression and access to information; Assess the potential financial impacts of age assurance on businesses, including micro and small enterprises. The study was carried out by an external contractor. It does not assess the proposed EU KIDS Act and the compliance by any specific service provider. The study's key insights are: Fundamental rights – an age assurance framework can be both proportionate and respectful of fundamental rights. Interferences with those rights can be mitigated through appropriate safeguards. In particular, the framework should ensure: Data protection and privacy – legislative coherence with the GDPR, high standards of privacy and security, and the development of technical standards; Non-discrimination, freedom of expression and access to information – minimising friction for users, ensuring transparency, promoting user empowerment where appropriate through greater choice, and ensuring inclusivity and accessibility. EU approach to age verification – the EU age verification blueprint can make an important contribution to the development of a coherent EU-level approach to age assurance. Specifically, the findings suggest that: the blueprint has the potential to become one of the most affordable ways for service providers of all sizes to comply with age assurance requirements because it is privacy-preserving and open by design and its development costs have been publicly subsidised; the roll-out of the blueprint across all Member States should be accelerated; the provision and resourcing of effective fallback enrollment routes – including manual enrolment options at national and local level – should be ensured. Costs for businesses – online services would inevitably face new costs. However, these costs are likely to remain modest for most services and to decrease over time, due to: competition in the third-party vendor market, the emergence of technical standards, improvements in interoperability, the availability of the EU age verification blueprint. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the study suggests that it's unlikely to face excessive costs, thanks to affordable, ready-to-use age verification solutions and competition between providers. They will also benefit from having a common set of EU rules, rather than having to comply with different national requirements. Read the study and its executive summary and the questions & answers on the proposed EU KIDS Act. Related topics Online platforms and e-commerce DSA - Digital Services Act

nodes.title: Call for evidence on advertising repositories
nodes.tldr: Call for evidence on advertising repositories Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 11:10   Opening: 04 November 2026   Closing: 02 December 2026 The Commission is s...
nodes.details: Call for evidence on advertising repositories Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 11:10   Opening: 04 November 2026   Closing: 02 December 2026 The Commission is seeking feedback on upcoming technical guidelines concerning advertising repositories under the Digital Services Act (DSA). The feedback is being gathered through a call for evidence. The responses collected through the call for evidence will help shape guidelines aimed at ensuring that advertising repositories meet the needs of their users. Amongst other things, the guidelines will advise on: how to make advertising repositories easily searchable how to provide insights on how users are targeted and reached how to make the content of advertisements accessible Once adopted, these guidelines will aim to ensure that the advertising repositories provided by very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) are effective and fit for purpose. Effective advertising repositories are essential tools for enabling greater public scrutiny of online advertising. Transparency in advertising – revealing who pays and how citizens are targeted – helps to protect public health, ensure a high level of consumer protection and safeguard the integrity of elections. Advertising repositories also support effective supervision and enforcement of the DSA. Next steps The call for evidence will be followed by a targeted public consultation in 2027. Researchers, civil society, providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs and representatives from the advertising industry will be invited to share feedback on a draft version of the guidelines. The publication of the guidelines is planned for the second quarter of 2028. Background Under Article 39 of the DSA, providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs are required to maintain publicly accessible repositories of advertisements displayed on their services. These repositories (commonly known as ‘ad libraries’) provide information on the content of advertisements, who paid for them, the period during which they were displayed, how many users the advertisements reached, and the main criteria used to decide who saw the advertisements. Article 39(3) of the DSA provides the possibility for the Commission to issue guidelines on the design of advertising repositories, following consultation with the European Board for Digital Services, researchers and the public. The guidelines will support the Commission’s supervision and enforcement of VLOPs and VLOSEs’ compliance with Article 39 of the DSA.
